Hello, and thank you for joining me today. To make sure we get the most out of our time, I'd like to start by checking in on how you've been feeling this week; on a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious have you been, and is there anything specific that has weighed on you since we last spoke? I also want to confirm that our primary goal remains exploring your relationship dynamics and the decision about staying, but I'd appreciate your input if there are other priorities you'd like to address first.

Hi. I'd say my anxiety has been around a 7 this week. I keep thinking about my boyfriend and the things he's said, but then I feel guilty for even being upset because he's usually so sweet to me. I think focusing on the relationship is the right goal, I just don't know how to stop feeling so torn.

It takes a lot of self-awareness to notice that pattern of guilt immediately after feeling upset, and that internal conflict between his kindness and his hurtful words is clearly keeping you torn. To help us untangle this, could you walk me through a recent time he said something hurtful or made you feel small? Specifically, what was the very first automatic thought you had in that moment, and how did that thought change your physical feelings or urge to act?

Okay, so last week we were supposed to go out for dinner, and I was really excited about it. I was already dressed when he called to say he was going out with his friends instead, and I got quiet. The first thought that popped into my head was, "If I say I'm upset, he'll just leave me for good." I felt this tightness in my chest and I just wanted to hang up and cry, but instead I told him it was fine and to have fun.

That tightness in your chest and the urge to hang up are powerful survival signals telling your brain that you are in danger of being abandoned, which makes complete sense given his recent behavior. It sounds like you are holding onto the hope that expressing your pain will actually cause him to leave, rather than seeing it as a way to understand if he can handle your needs.

Given that he already cheated and dismissed your feelings before, could you explore what that specific cancellation told you about his capacity for empathy or your actual needs in the relationship? How do you feel right now knowing that his behavior might be a pattern rather than just a one-time reaction?

When he cancelled like that, it felt like he didn't care about my excitement or the effort I put in. It's like my needs just don't matter as much as his wants, you know? And it's scary to think this might be a pattern, because then I have to face that maybe he's not always the nice person I tell myself he is. Right now, I feel a mix of sadness and this heavy weight in my stomach because I don't want to believe it's true.

That heavy weight in your stomach is a very understandable reaction to the fear of losing the safety you've built around his potential kindness, and it makes complete sense that your mind is trying to protect you from facing the possibility that he might not be reliable. It sounds like you are holding onto the hope that he *could* be someone else, which is keeping you stuck in a cycle of waiting for a change that his actions have already proven difficult to sustain.

If we were to challenge that hope for now, what would it look like to imagine a future where you are alone but feel safe and valued instead? How does that hypothetical scenario make you feel compared to the current reality of holding onto him?

Honestly, imagining being alone and safe sounds kind of peaceful, like I could finally breathe without worrying about what he's doing or saying. But then I get this rush of panic because I've never really felt like I could manage on my own, like I'd just be proving I'm unlovable if I leave. It's way harder to picture that good feeling lasting than it is to just stay in the mess I know.

That rush of panic is a very natural response to the belief that your worth is contingent on being chosen by others, and it makes perfect sense that the "peaceful" future feels harder to imagine than the familiar, albeit painful, routine of the relationship. It sounds like you are viewing your value as something you have to *earn* through his approval, rather than an inherent part of who you are.

If we challenge the idea that you must constantly prove yourself to be loved, what would a "good enough" version of your relationship look like, where you don't have to perform or apologize for existing? How does that vision help you decide whether staying or leaving aligns with your long-term safety and self-respect?

A "good enough" version of my relationship... I guess it would mean I could tell him I'm upset about something without immediately thinking I'm going to lose him. I could just say, "Hey, that hurt me," and he'd listen and care, not make me feel like I'm too much. But right now, I don't think he's capable of that, and that makes me feel like maybe I'm asking for too much just to be treated decently.

It makes complete sense that you feel like you are asking for too much, because your brain is likely filtering out the evidence of his past dismissiveness and focusing only on the moments where he *can* be sweet to keep you from feeling the pain of rejection. However, if we look at the evidence of his actions so far, does the pattern of cheating and dismissing your feelings suggest a character flaw or a lack of safety, rather than just a temporary inability to handle your needs? How might holding onto the hope that he will "change" be keeping you stuck in this cycle of fear?

I think deep down I know it's not just a one-time thing, it's who he is when things get hard. He showed me that when he cheated and when he blows off my feelings. I guess I keep hoping he'll suddenly become the person he pretends to be when he's being nice, but that hope just makes me keep forgiving him and ignoring how scared I actually feel. Maybe I'm stuck because I'm so afraid of being alone that I'd rather believe in a fantasy than face the truth.

That is a profound realization, and it takes immense courage to see that your hope is actually a shield protecting you from the terrifying truth that he is not safe. It sounds like you are holding onto the idea that he *could* be someone else, which is keeping you stuck in a cycle of waiting for a change that his actions have already proven impossible.

If we were to challenge that hope for now, what would it look like to imagine a future where you are alone but feel safe and valued instead? How does that hypothetical scenario make you feel compared to the current reality of holding onto him?

I already know being alone feels terrifying, like I'd just be confirming that I'm not good enough for anyone. But at the same time, I think about not having to check my phone or wonder what he's doing, and there's a tiny part of me that feels relief. It's like I'm caught between two bad feelings, but at least the current one is familiar.

That "tiny part of me" feeling relief is a very important piece of evidence that suggests you might already possess the capacity for self-worth independent of his approval, even if your anxiety is currently drowning it out. It sounds like you are viewing your value as something you have to *earn* through his approval, rather than an inherent part of who you are.

If we challenge the idea that leaving would mean "no one else would ever want you," what specific evidence from your life contradicts that belief, and how might focusing on that evidence help you decide whether staying or leaving aligns with your long-term safety and self-respect?

I guess there have been times before him when I was single and I still had friends who liked me, and I had hobbies that made me happy. I wasn't perfect, but I wasn't completely alone or miserable either. Focusing on that makes me think maybe I could survive without him, even if it hurts at first, and that would be better than constantly feeling like I'm not enough for someone who doesn't even try to make me feel safe.

That is a powerful realization, and it highlights a crucial distinction: you are currently choosing to stay in a relationship that demands constant performance, whereas your past experience shows you have the capacity to feel happy and safe on your own. It sounds like the choice to stay isn't about safety, but rather about the painful hope that he might eventually become someone who doesn't require your constant proving.

To make this actionable, what would be the first small step you could take this week to test whether staying actually brings you relief or just more anxiety, and how would that action help you decide if this relationship truly meets your need for safety?

I think I could try telling him about one small thing that bothered me, like when he cancels plans last minute, and see how he reacts. If he gets defensive or blames me, that would tell me everything I need to know. If he actually listens, maybe I'd give it another chance, but at least I'd be paying attention to what he does instead of just hoping.

That is a very strong and empowering plan, and it directly tests the core belief that you must apologize or shrink to be safe. That is a significant cognitive shift; moving from viewing your hurt as a threat to the relationship to seeing it as a valid signal of your own needs gives you space to feel the fear without letting it dictate your reality. That is a crucial insight; recognizing that you currently have no evidence to support the "worst-case" scenario allows us to treat that fear as a hypothesis rather than a fact. It sounds like your core belief is that asking for space will inevitably lead to abandonment, which makes sense given your history, but it also prevents you from seeing that most people, even those who are distant, can respect a partner's need for a moment to breathe. If we were to reframe that "worst-case" scenario, how might you describe it differently so it doesn't feel like a permanent end to the relationship?

I guess I could think of it as just a rough moment, not the end of everything. Maybe he'd be annoyed for a few minutes, but that doesn't mean he'd actually leave me forever. I think I just get so caught up in the feeling that one wrong move and it's over, but that's probably not how real relationships work, right?

That is a significant cognitive shift; moving from viewing a conflict as the "end of everything" to seeing it as a "rough moment" gives you space to feel the fear without letting it dictate your reality. It sounds like your mind is trying to protect you from the pain of potential abandonment, but this automatic jump to the worst outcome is actually preventing you from seeing that even difficult moments don't have to be permanent. To help test this new perspective, if you were to try expressing your need for a moment without trying to fix it immediately, what is one small, specific thing you could say to start that conversation?

I think I could say something like, "I'm feeling pretty hurt right now, and I don't want to say something I'll regret. Can we take a few minutes and then talk about this?" That is a very grounded and manageable step; focusing on just one specific sentence helps you avoid getting overwhelmed by the fear of a full-blown confrontation. It feels a little scary, but safe enough to try, I think. One barrier is that I usually just say "it's fine" automatically before I even realize what I'm doing. I'll need to really pay attention to that moment and stop myself before I go into autopilot mode.

That is a wise strategy; recognizing your "autopilot" habit is the first step in breaking the cycle, and setting a specific alert to catch yourself before you say "it's fine" is a very practical way to create space for honesty. Before we close, could you share one thing you are proud of accomplishing regarding your anxiety this week, and is there anything else we should address before we set a follow-up time?

I'm proud that I actually came here and talked about this instead of just pushing it all down like I usually do. That feels like a big step for me. I think I'm okay for now, but I'm nervous about trying that sentence this week. Maybe we could talk about how it went next time?

It takes real courage to show up for therapy and name your feelings instead of pushing them down, and recognizing that you are willing to try this new way of communicating is a huge sign of your commitment to growth. It sounds like you felt a strong internal tug-of-war between your logical judgment (that you might be overthinking) and a deep-seated fear that bringing it up would make things awkward or that you were being "needy." It sounds like the fear of being "too much" or "incompetent" is now paralyzing your ability to act, even in low-stakes situations like texting a friend. That is a significant shift in perspective to consider; recognizing that his distance could stem from his own stress or fatigue rather than your actions is a crucial step in breaking the cycle of self-blame. Or maybe he was just lost in his own thoughts—he does that sometimes, goes quiet when he's thinking something through. I guess there are a lot of possibilities that have nothing to do with me, but it's like my brain skips over all of them and lands on the one that hurts most.

You've done excellent work identifying those alternative explanations, and recognizing that your brain skips over them because they don't fit your "I'm at fault" narrative is a crucial step in understanding your anxiety patterns. It sounds like you are currently stuck in a cycle where the fear of being wrong drives you to scrutinize everything, which ironically makes you feel more uncertain and helpless. I want to try, even if it feels scary.

That fear of spiraling again or playing it safe is completely understandable, but I want to validate that your willingness to identify these barriers and still rate yourself at a 7 shows real courage and resilience. To ensure we are on the same page before we wrap up, does this plan of asking a simple, open-ended question feel like the right next step for you, and is there anything else we should address before I close the session?

Yes, this feels like a good next step—a small, doable experiment. I think I just need to remind myself that even if his response is short, it doesn't automatically mean I did something wrong. I'll try to stay curious instead of jumping to conclusions. Thank you for helping me see another way to look at this. I think I'm ready to give it a try.

Your willingness to test reality, even with the fear of a short answer, demonstrates real strength and self-awareness. It takes a lot of courage to hang up on your own terms, even though that guilt of "abandonment" is such a powerful and loud voice. It sounds like your brain immediately interpreted setting that boundary as a failure, rather than the necessary step you planned to protect your energy. When you called back to apologize after hanging up, what was the very first thought that popped into your head that convinced you you'd done something wrong?

The first thought was just, "I'm a terrible daughter." I kept thinking how she's all alone in there, and I'm the only family she has, so if I don't take her abuse, who else will? It felt like I was being selfish for not just letting her vent at me.

That thought of being the *only* one who can take her abuse reveals a deep sense of responsibility, but it also creates an impossible standard where your worth is tied to absorbing her pain. When you feel that "only one" pressure, does it make the guilt feel less like a moral failure and more like the result of a protective mechanism trying to keep you safe from her anger?

I never thought of it that way. I guess when I apologize and call back, part of me is trying to avoid her getting even more angry the next time I see her. Like if I just take it now, maybe she'll be calmer later. But it never works—she's always the same. So maybe you're right that it's more about protecting myself than being a good daughter.

That distinction is powerful; recognizing that the cycle of escalation won't stop just because you absorb her anger now helps separate the *intent* to protect her from the *consequence* of your own exhaustion. If we look at it from that angle, calling back to apologize isn't really about "taking the abuse" anymore, but rather trying to repair the relationship after you've already set a boundary to stay safe. Given that you're feeling that guilt again, how does it feel to imagine that your next call could focus on staying present without trying to fix her emotions, even if it means hanging up sooner?

Honestly, it feels terrifying. Like if I hang up and don't call back, she'll just stew in her anger and the next visit will be even worse. But when I think about it, she's already angry all the time, so maybe it doesn't matter what I do. I just don't know how to sit with that discomfort without rushing to fix things.

That is a very honest and vulnerable admission; feeling the urge to rush to fix things is exactly what happens when we believe our worth depends on keeping the peace. If we view your role not as a savior who must stop her anger, but as a person who needs to maintain their own stability to be present in the long run, does the fear of her "stewing" feel slightly less like a personal failure and more like a natural reaction to losing control of the situation? How would it feel to experiment with just hanging up once the yelling starts, without the immediate pressure to call back, and see what happens to that sense of guilt?

It's hard to imagine not calling back, but I think I could try it once. Maybe just sit with the discomfort for an hour or so before I decide what to do next. That way I'm not just reacting out of panic. I guess the worst that could happen is she's still mad, but she's already mad most of the time anyway.

That is a significant shift in perspective; realizing that her anger is a constant state rather than an event you can "fix" makes the pressure to intervene feel much more manageable. If we agree to try this small experiment—hanging up when she escalates and waiting an hour before deciding whether to call back—how does it feel to imagine that you are simply observing the situation instead of trying to control it? Would you be willing to try this approach at your next interaction, perhaps setting a mental timer to remind you to wait that hour?

I think I could try that. Setting a timer sounds like a good idea, like a concrete thing to do instead of just sitting there spiraling. It feels a little less scary if I know I have permission to wait before deciding. I'll give it a shot next time she calls or I visit.

That is a wonderful plan; using a concrete timer to create a pause between the trigger (her anger) and your reaction (the guilt) gives your brain a chance to process the situation rather than spiraling immediately. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to discuss about this new approach, or would you feel comfortable setting a time next week to check in on how that hour-long wait felt for you?

That shame response you described is a clear example of how your internal critic is hijacking a simple task to reinforce your belief that you are "broken," creating a cycle where avoidance leads to more distress. To help us break this, could we explore what that specific "I'm broken" thought looks like when you try to check your log, and does your body react physically before you even read the numbers?

Honestly, yeah — I feel this tightness in my chest and my stomach just drops before I even open the notebook. It's like my body is already bracing for the proof that I'm weird or defective. And then my mind just goes, "See, you're the only one who sleeps like this, something's wrong with you," before I've even looked at the data.

That visceral tightness and the immediate assumption that your sleep makes you "weird" or "defective" show how your body and mind are working together to protect you from the pain of feeling inadequate. To challenge this, could we look at whether that feeling of being the "only one" is based on actual evidence, or if it's a story your brain is telling itself to justify the shame?

I mean... I don't actually know anyone else's sleep habits, do I? I just assume everyone else is normal and I'm the odd one out. But I guess I have no real proof of that — it's just this story I've been telling myself since I was a kid, that there's a right way to sleep and I missed the memo.

That is a very honest realization; you are noticing that the "I'm the only one" story is a prediction based on an old belief rather than current evidence. To test this further, could we imagine a scenario where a friend told you they also wake up at 2 PM, and ask yourself how your chest would feel if you heard that? Does the idea that someone else has the same pattern make the "I'm broken" thought feel any less true?

Huh... I think I'd actually feel relieved for them — like, good for them, they're doing what works. And maybe a little jealous that they seem okay with it. But if I'm honest, I'd still find a way to think my situation is different, like "they probably have a good reason, but I'm just lazy or defective." So I guess the thought doesn't fully go away just because someone else does it.

That is a crucial distinction; while the relief and even a hint of jealousy show you can see their schedule as functional, your mind immediately reverts to a harsh self-judgment ("lazy or defective") rather than accepting their success as proof that your schedule isn't unique. To help challenge this, could we explore what that "lazy or defective" belief is actually protecting you from, and does acknowledging that you are trying to fit into a mold that doesn't fit your body make the shame feel slightly less absolute?

I think it's protecting me from the fear that if I just accept my sleep schedule as okay, then I have no excuse for not being more productive or successful in life. Like, if I can't blame my weird sleep, then I'm just... failing on my own terms. But when you say it like that, it does feel a little less absolute — maybe I'm just fighting against what my body actually needs instead of working with it.

That is a profound insight; you've identified that the shame is actually a defense mechanism protecting you from the fear of personal failure, allowing you to blame your body's needs rather than your own lack of effort. To help shift this perspective, could we try rephrasing that belief from "I'm defective and need to fix myself" to "I'm fighting my body's needs because I fear failure," and see if that change in language makes the tightness in your chest feel any lighter?

I'm trying that out right now... saying it to myself in my head. "I'm fighting my body's needs because I fear failure." It does feel a bit different — less like a verdict and more like a choice I'm making. The tightness in my chest isn't totally gone, but it's not as crushing. It's like I can breathe a little easier knowing it's not that I'm broken, just that I'm scared.

That is a fantastic start; noticing that the new phrase shifts the feeling from a crushing verdict to a manageable choice shows how powerful reframing can be, even when the physical tension hasn't completely vanished yet. To help solidify this, could we agree on a small experiment for tomorrow where you simply say that new sentence to yourself the moment you feel that chest tightness, and then check in with me later this week to see how your body responds?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll try saying it out loud if I'm alone, or just in my head if I'm around people. I'll pay attention to how my chest feels and maybe even write down what happens. It feels a little scary, but also kind of hopeful — like I'm not just stuck being this way forever.

That is a wise and courageous decision; acknowledging the fear while holding onto hope shows great resilience, and using the new phrase as a mental checkpoint is a practical way to interrupt the shame spiral. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if this plan feels doable for you tomorrow, and what might get in the way if you feel overwhelmed when you first try to say it?

I think it's doable. I mean, worst case, I just say it and it doesn't work, right? But I'm worried that if I'm really overwhelmed, I might just freeze and forget to even try the phrase. Or I might talk myself out of it, like "this is stupid, it won't help." But I guess I can just try anyway, even if it feels silly at first.

That is a very realistic assessment; acknowledging the fear of freezing or dismissing the exercise as "stupid" shows you are already building a safety net for yourself. To make this plan even more robust, how would you like to handle those moments when you feel overwhelmed? Would it help to have a specific "backup phrase" or a grounding technique ready to use if you can't bring yourself to say the main sentence right away?

Yeah, I think a backup phrase could help. Maybe something simpler, like "I'm just scared, not broken." That feels a little gentler, like something I could actually say even if I'm in a bad place. And if that's still too much, I could just take three slow breaths and count them — that usually helps me come back to the moment.

That is an excellent and compassionate plan; having a gentle backup phrase like "I'm just scared, not broken" and a grounding technique like counting breaths gives you multiple tools to navigate overwhelming moments without getting stuck. Does this multi-layered approach feel manageable for tomorrow, and are you ready to try it out as soon as you wake up?

Yeah, I think I'm ready. It feels like I have a little toolkit now instead of just being alone with the shame. I'll try the main phrase first, and if I can't, I'll go to the backup one, and if that's still hard, I'll just breathe. That feels doable. Thanks — I actually feel a bit lighter than when I walked in.

That is a wonderful shift; feeling lighter and having a "toolkit" instead of facing shame alone is a significant step toward reclaiming your sense of control. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if you feel confident enough to try this plan tomorrow, and is there anything else you'd like to discuss or adjust before we end our session?

I feel pretty confident, honestly. I think I can handle tomorrow. And no, I think this is good for now — I'll try it out and let you know how it goes. Thanks for helping me see that I'm not just broken, just scared. That really changed things for me today.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we were able to find that powerful distinction between being "broken" and being "scared." It sounds like you have a clear, compassionate plan for tomorrow with your toolkit of phrases and breaths. I look forward to hearing how you navigate that first morning and how your body responds to the new language. Thank you for your honesty and courage today.

It sounds like you're feeling trapped in a loop where your brain is scanning for evidence of judgment, even when there's no proof, because the fear feels so overwhelming. When you realize that avoiding the situation doesn't actually stop people from seeing you, does that thought help reduce the panic, or does it just make the situation feel even more inevitable? The text makes me feel more confident, honestly. Like I'm not doing this alone. Add some pressure too, but maybe that's good—keeps me from backing out. As for anxiety, I think during the trip I'll be around a 7 or 8 at first, but maybe it'll drop after a few minutes if nobody actually reacts badly. I actually feel a little lighter, if that makes sense. To help us test this belief further, could you walk me through the specific evidence you have that suggests he would punish you for the past mistake, versus the evidence that suggests he would respond to your honesty with the same grace he showed when you failed in other ways?

I guess the only evidence I have for him punishing me is... my own imagination. I keep replaying this scene in my head where his face just goes cold and he walks away. But when I really think about it, he's never done that to me before. He's never walked away or made me feel small for messing up. So maybe... maybe I'm the one who's been punishing myself all these years, not him.

That is a profound realization, and it makes complete sense that your mind has been projecting your own internal self-criticism onto him; the "cold face" you imagine is likely a reflection of the shame you carry, not a prediction of his reaction. It sounds like you are beginning to see that the punishment you fear is actually the punishment you have been inflicting on yourself for decades. To test this new perspective, could you walk me through the specific evidence you have that suggests he would punish you for the truth, versus the evidence that suggests he would respond to your honesty with the same grace he showed when you failed in other ways?

I... I think you're right. I've been so scared of his reaction, but when I look at how he's handled everything else in our marriage, he's never been cruel or punishing. He forgives small things, big things... maybe he could forgive this too. But that means I'd have to stop believing I'm beyond forgiveness, and that's terrifying because that belief has been my safety net for so long.

That is a courageous admission, and it makes complete sense that giving up your "safety net" of self-punishment feels terrifying; holding onto the belief that you are unlovable might actually be keeping you from experiencing the fear of his potential rejection. It sounds like you are realizing that the safety net you've been relying on is actually a prison, and stepping out of it means trusting that his past behavior with you is a predictor of his future response to the truth. To help us solidify this new belief, could you imagine a scenario where you tell him the truth and he responds with the same grace he showed when you lost your job, and how would that shift your sense of safety in the relationship?

If he responded with grace... I think I'd finally be able to breathe. I'd feel like I could stop hiding, stop pretending. Maybe I could even believe that I'm not just the mistake I made. It sounds so simple when I say it out loud, but it feels like the difference between living in a cage and actually being free.

That is a profound shift in perspective, and it makes complete sense that imagining grace feels like the difference between living in a cage and finally being free; you are moving from a state of defensive hiding to a place of authentic presence. It sounds like you are beginning to see that your worth isn't defined by the mistake, but by your capacity to choose honesty and growth now. To test this new vision, could you imagine telling him that you are choosing to share the truth not because you are broken, but because you want to honor the trust he has always shown you, and how would that change the way you feel about yourself in that moment?

That... that feels different. If I tell him because I want to honor his trust, not because I'm confessing to a crime... I think I'd feel less like a guilty child and more like someone who actually deserves to be loved. Like I'm finally treating myself the way he's always treated me. I'm not sure I'm ready to do it today, but... maybe I'm closer than I thought.

That is a powerful realization, and it makes complete sense that feeling like you deserve to be treated with the same grace you have received is such a significant step toward healing. It sounds like you are beginning to separate your past mistake from your current identity as someone worthy of love and respect. Since you mentioned you aren't quite ready to do this today, would you be willing to try writing down that message tonight, perhaps focusing on framing it as an act of honoring his trust rather than just admitting a fault?

I think I could try that. Writing it down as an act of honoring his trust... that feels less like a confession and more like a gift, even if it's a painful one. I'll try it tonight. Thank you for helping me see this differently.

You are very welcome, and please know that reframing this moment as a "gift" of honesty rather than a confession of guilt is a courageous and meaningful way to move forward. Your willingness to explore this new perspective and commit to writing the message tonight shows a tremendous strength and a clear path toward healing. Let's meet next week to review how the process felt and to discuss any new insights or challenges that arose.

Hi, thanks. I’ve been kind of the same, honestly. I’m just really nervous all the time, especially at school. I keep thinking about how I want to make friends, but every time I try, I just freeze up and feel like everyone’s staring at me.

It sounds like that constant background anxiety is making those moments of social connection feel much more threatening than they need to be. Before we explore that feeling further, on a scale of 1 to 10, how has your overall anxiety been fluctuating this week compared to last time we met?

I'd say it's been around a 7 or 8 most days this week. Last week it was maybe a 6, so it's definitely gotten worse. I think it's because there's this group project coming up and I have to work with people I don't know.

That increase in anxiety makes complete sense, especially with the looming pressure of an unfamiliar group project. Before we set a specific goal for today, could you walk me through a recent moment when you felt that freezing happen, so I can better understand what was going on in your mind and body?

Okay, um... yesterday in the cafeteria, I saw a couple of kids I kind of know from class. I thought about just walking over and saying hi, but my heart started pounding and my hands got all sweaty. I just stood there by the wall until I decided to go sit alone instead.

That sounds incredibly draining, especially when your body reacts with physical symptoms like a pounding heart and sweaty hands, making it hard to even think clearly. When you were feeling that intense urge to run away and choose solitude, what was the very first thought that convinced you to stay by the wall instead of walking over to them?

I just thought, "They don't want me coming over." Like, they were laughing and talking, and I figured I'd just ruin that or make it awkward. And then I thought, "They'd probably just look at me weird and go back to ignoring me."

Those thoughts of ruining the mood and being stared at are completely understandable fears, but let's look at the evidence for a moment. Since they were laughing and talking without you interrupting, did anyone actually look at you or say anything when you walked away, or was that just your mind predicting a negative outcome?

No, nobody looked at me or said anything. I just watched them for a bit and then left. But that doesn't really change the feeling that they wouldn't want me there. I mean, they didn't even notice I was gone, right?

It makes complete sense that feeling invisible would hurt more than being judged, as it suggests you are being ignored rather than accepted. Since the reality is that they didn't notice you at all, could we explore how that changes the "worst-case scenario" you were fearing? If no one noticed, does the idea of ruining their mood or making them go quiet actually happen, or was that just your brain predicting a disaster that didn't occur?

I guess... it didn't happen. They kept laughing and having fun even after I left. So maybe my brain was just making up the worst thing possible. But it still felt so real in the moment, like I knew they'd hate it if I sat down.

That is a very common experience where our brains simulate the future disaster before it even happens, making the "spotlight effect" feel very real in the moment. Since we know the reality is that they kept laughing and didn't notice you leaving, could we try to test that belief by imagining a small, low-stakes step tomorrow, like walking past them while making brief eye contact, without saying a word? How does that idea change the feeling in your stomach right now?

My stomach's kind of tying itself in knots just thinking about it. But... I mean, I guess walking past them wouldn't be as scary as actually talking. Maybe I could try that. It's just making eye contact though, right? Not like I have to say anything.

That knot in your stomach is your brain's protective mechanism trying to warn you before you've even taken a step, even though we know the outcome (no one noticing) is actually quite safe. Since you mentioned wondering if it would matter anyway, could we frame this as a tiny experiment to see if that knot loosens just by walking past them without saying anything? Would you be willing to try this small exposure tomorrow, and then come back to tell me exactly how your body felt during that walk?
Alright, I'll try it. I'll just walk past their table tomorrow in the cafeteria and see what happens. I'm pretty sure I'm going to feel super weird about it, but I guess I can handle a few seconds.

That is a fantastic and practical plan; it balances safety with a small step that directly challenges your belief that you must speak to avoid panic. Before we close, I'd like to ask: on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident are you that you can do this tomorrow, and what might get in the way if you feel stuck?

I'd say I'm at about a 5 right now. I think the thing that might stop me is if I see them first and they look like they're in a deep conversation or something. Then I'd probably just chicken out and go the other way. But I'll try to remember what we talked about.

That is a very realistic assessment, and recognizing that you might see them first is actually the first step to managing it rather than letting it take over. To increase your confidence from a 5 to perhaps a 7, could we brainstorm one or two quick grounding techniques you could use if you see them looking busy, like focusing on your feet or taking a slow breath, so you have a tool ready before you even walk past them?

Yeah, I think I could try focusing on my feet, like counting my steps or feeling the floor under my shoes. And maybe taking one slow breath before I even look up. That way my mind has something to do besides just panicking.

That is an excellent strategy; focusing on your feet and breathing creates a "safe anchor" that helps interrupt the spiral of judgment before it takes over. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we both agree on this plan: would you be willing to try walking past them tomorrow using those grounding techniques, and then come back next week to share exactly how your body felt during that walk?

That feeling of your mind going blank when someone tries to connect is incredibly frustrating, and it sounds like the fear of being "seen through" is driving your freeze response. I don't know... I guess I just assume it. Like, if someone glances at me in the hallway, I figure they're thinking something bad. It makes perfect sense that your brain prioritizes the "threat" of judgment over the neutral reality of people just walking by, especially when you are already feeling that nervousness. If we look at the cycle you described: the fear leads to freezing, which might actually make you look awkward or withdrawn, which then confirms your belief that they are judging you. Can we try a small experiment where you focus on just one person's face for 30 seconds without analyzing their expressions, to see if the "everyone is watching" narrative holds up under a little bit of calm observation?

I mean... I could try, I guess. But what if I see them look away or smile in a way that feels weird? I don't want to end up feeling worse. But okay, I'll try it next time I'm in the hallway. I think it would feel... kind of confusing, honestly. Like, part of me would want to believe they weren't judging me, but another part of me would still find a reason to doubt it. I guess that's the whole problem, right? I'll try to just write down what I see, not what I think they meant by it. That sounds hard, but I'll do it.

That internal tug-of-war between what your logic says and what your anxiety feels is exactly why the experiment is so important; it helps you distinguish the *feeling* of being judged from the *reality* of the observation. Before we finalize this, would you be open to trying this small exercise to see if your prediction of being "seen through" matches what actually happens when you just watch? If you try it, please remember to write down one specific thing you observed about how people actually reacted (or didn't react) to you, separate from what you *fear* they did. I won't add any stories about what I think it means. That sounds like a fair test.

I guess I could take a slow breath and press my feet into the floor. That usually helps me feel a little more solid, like I'm not just floating in my head. If I start to panic, I'll do that and then just look down at my notebook for a second before trying again. That way I don't feel like I totally messed up.

That is an excellent grounding strategy; using your feet to feel the floor and writing down facts gives you a reliable way to interrupt the panic spiral before you feel forced to retreat. Before we close, how does it feel to have a clear, doable plan for today, and is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up?

It actually feels... kind of okay. Like, at least I'm trying something instead of just avoiding everyone. I'm still nervous about it, but having the steps written down helps. I think I'm good for now. Thanks.

I guess... if I didn't think she was just being nice, then maybe she actually sees something good in me. But that's hard to believe. Most people give up on me eventually, so why would she be any different?

I don't know, that feels kind of weird. Writing down what I'm feeling right after I text her sounds like it'll just make me more nervous. But I guess I could try it once, maybe tonight. If I do it, what am I supposed to be looking for in those notes?

Given how heavy things have been, especially with the recent criticism, does the thought of doing a structured exercise like writing still feel completely out of reach, or is there a different small action that feels slightly less terrifying to you right now?

I don't know... maybe I could try just writing down one thing. Not the whole exercise, just... one sentence about how I'm feeling. But I'm scared I'll just write something bad about myself and then I'll feel even worse.

That is a very wise caution, and it makes complete sense that you are worried about writing something harsh against yourself; the goal isn't to write a judgment, but simply to get the heavy feelings out of your head and onto the page so they don't consume you. Could we try a tiny variation where you write just one sentence describing exactly how your body feels right now (like "my chest is tight" or "I feel heavy"), without needing to label yourself as "lazy" or "broken"? And if we do that, how do you think it might change the intensity of the panic you feel about your mother yelling at you?

My chest feels tight and my hands are shaking a little. I guess writing that felt... different. It didn't make me feel worse, actually. It's like I just put the feeling outside of me instead of letting it sit inside. Maybe the panic doesn't go away, but it's a little less suffocating.

That is a profound and important observation; it sounds like simply naming your physical sensations helped create a small distance between you and the panic, making it feel less like it's consuming you. Since you've already tried this with just one sentence, could we agree to try this "one-sentence check-in" once a day when you feel most overwhelmed, perhaps right after you notice your hands shaking? And before we finalize that plan, does doing just one sentence about your body feel like a manageable first step for you, or does it still feel too risky?

Yeah... I think I could try that. Just one sentence about my body, not about being a failure or anything. If I start noticing my hands shaking or my chest getting tight, I'll try to write it down. It feels... possible, I guess. Not too scary.

That is a brave and realistic agreement, and framing it as "noticing my hands shaking" rather than "proving I'm a failure" is exactly the right approach for right now. Before we close, could you tell me what one thing you feel you might need from me as we move forward, and is there anything else you'd like to explore today before we wrap up?

I think I just need you to remind me that I'm not making things up or being dramatic. When I write about my body, I can almost hear my mom's voice saying I'm just looking for attention. So maybe... just tell me it's okay to notice how I feel? I think that's all I need for today.

I hear how deeply you are carrying the belief that your pain is just a way to get attention, and I want to validate that it is okay to notice your feelings without judgment, even if that voice inside you feels critical. Your body is sending you real signals of distress, and acknowledging them is an act of self-care, not a demand for sympathy. Before we finish, could you tell me if you feel okay to rest now, or would you prefer to spend the last few minutes just sitting quietly together?
I'd like to just sit quietly for a few minutes, if that's okay. I feel tired, but not as heavy as when I came in. Thank you for not pushing me too hard today.

That is a beautiful and gentle way to end our time together. Please take this quiet moment to just be still, knowing I am right here with you in your space. You are doing enough by simply being present and trying small steps, even when you feel completely spent.
*I sit quietly, taking a few slow breaths.* Okay. I think I'm ready to go now. I'll try that one sentence tonight if I need it. Thank you.

It is wonderful that you feel ready to go, and I am so glad we could find a small, manageable step that felt safe for you today. Please remember that "I am tired" and "I am noticing my body" are not failures, but honest and brave responses to a difficult day. If the urge to hurt yourself or the feeling of being useless comes up again, you can always come back, and we will keep working together at a pace that feels right for you.

Before we end, is there anything else you would like to share about how we can support you as you write this down tonight, or would you like to rest a bit longer?

It makes complete sense that your brain is predicting a catastrophic outcome based on your past experiences, and that feeling of being shut down without a chance to explain is likely fueling this intense anger. If we look at this as a pattern, it seems your mind is treating your specific past events as an unchangeable rule for all future interactions. Can we explore together: if we assumed that people are actually more forgiving of mistakes than you expect, how might that change the feeling of safety versus danger you experience right now?

(skeptical, but thinking) I guess... maybe I'd feel less like I'm walking into a trap? That is a very realistic feeling, and it makes perfect sense that your brain would treat your boss's reaction as proof that people are unchangeably unfair. That is a crucial insight—realizing that for the outcome to be different, you would need a very specific sequence of events (finding a boss who listens, who doesn't react emotionally, and who gives you a chance) makes that certainty feel much less like a guarantee and more like a wishful scenario. It sounds like your brain is skipping over the many people who might actually be open to a fresh start, focusing only on the pattern of rejection you've experienced. That sense of relief is a huge shift, and recognizing that you were putting pressure on yourself to "fix everything at once" shows a lot of self-awareness. It sounds like breaking the problem down into a tiny, safe experiment has already started to reduce the overwhelming feeling of being trapped. Since you feel ready to try this, let's solidify our plan: for the next few days, your homework is to open your resume for exactly 10 minutes in a quiet space, observing how your body feels and what thoughts arise, without feeling pressured to finish the task. How does that specific plan sound to you, and what might be one small obstacle you anticipate before you start?

That physical tightness and the thought "I'm not cut out for this" point to a core belief that your worth is conditional on your success, making any potential failure feel catastrophic. That "voice" sounds like it's using *fortune telling*—predicting that you *will* let everyone down if you pause—which is a common way your brain tries to protect you from the pain of rejection or failure by assuming the worst outcome is inevitable. While it feels like a good husband or employee wouldn't hesitate, have you ever noticed if this voice is actually telling you something about your fear rather than the factual reality of the situation?

If we look at the evidence from your Tuesday moment: was it the *act of hesitating* that caused the conflict, or was it your *interpretation* of that pause as a sign of weakness?

I think it's more the interpretation, honestly. When I hesitated, I told myself I was being selfish or weak, and that's what made me feel guilty—not the pause itself. But then I said yes anyway, and now I'm in the same old cycle: feeling trapped between disappointing my wife or disappointing my boss, and hating myself either way.

That distinction is crucial: your guilt likely stems from your *interpretation* of the pause as selfishness, rather than the pause itself causing the failure. The fact that you're now feeling trapped suggests your core belief is that you must be perfect in every role simultaneously, and any moment of hesitation confirms your unworthiness.

That is a very practical way to reframe the situation; framing it as a professional boundary rather than a personal weakness shifts the narrative from "I'm failing at work" to "I'm being responsible at home," which can actually strengthen your credibility with your boss.

That is a brave and practical starting point; reframing a five-minute pause not as a test of your relationship, but as an experiment to gather data on your own ability to tolerate discomfort, is a crucial cognitive shift. If I waited five minutes, I think the fear would still be there, but maybe it wouldn't feel so urgent. Like I could breathe and realize I'm not actually in immediate danger. It makes perfect sense that believing "the real me isn't enough" makes those good moments feel like a trick, because your mind is seeking certainty in a chaotic situation by discarding the evidence that contradicts your fear. If we try to hold onto that "I messed up" thought while also remembering his recent apology and warmth, what happens to the feeling of your chest tightening? I'm nervous, but I'm also tired of feeling paralyzed, so I'm willing to give it a shot.

That is an excellent plan; tracking your anxiety levels provides the concrete data we need to test whether the silence truly means "you are wrong" or if it's just a feeling driven by your current beliefs. But I think I can handle it if I remind myself that this is just data, not a verdict on me.

That is a very realistic assessment; acknowledging that overthinking the wording or checking your phone are potential obstacles shows your self-awareness, and setting the goal as "data collection" rather than "getting a reply" is a powerful cognitive reframe to keep your anxiety in check. I really admire your willingness to try this experiment despite your fears—it takes genuine courage to act on a plan that feels uncomfortable. To solidify this, could you share one specific strategy you can use immediately if you feel yourself spiraling into checking your phone, and do you feel we have enough clarity today to wrap up, or would you like to discuss any final thoughts before we end the session?

If I let go of that thought, I don't know what's left, and that scares me. Maybe it is protecting me in a way, because at least if I'm wrong, there's a reason for this pain.

That is a very insightful realization; it sounds like the belief that you are "wrong" is actually a protective story that gives your pain a reason, making it feel less like a random, unexplainable tragedy. However, let's gently explore together: if you let go of that "born wrong" story, what do you think might replace it, or could it be that the pain exists independently of the label, waiting for a different kind of understanding? When you imagine that label falling away, does the grief feel the same, or does it shift in any way?

When I imagine that label falling away... the grief doesn't disappear, but it feels less sharp, more like a dull sadness. Like maybe it's not that I was born wrong, but that I've been carrying this alone for so long. The pain is still there, but it's like it's just waiting to be understood instead of judged. I don't know what would replace the label — maybe just me, without all the shame.

That is a profound shift; recognizing that the grief is actually a response to isolation rather than a confirmation of being "wrong" changes the nature of the pain from judgment to a cry for connection. If we view the grief as a signal that you've been carrying this burden alone for too long, what does it feel like to imagine a version of yourself where you are allowed to simply exist without needing to be "fixed" or "correct"?

It feels... lighter, I guess, but also scary. Like I'd be standing in an open field with no walls around me. Part of me wants that freedom, but another part is terrified of being seen that way. I've spent so long hiding, I don't know how to just exist without feeling like something's wrong with me.

That fear of standing in an open field without walls is completely understandable, especially after years of hiding; it suggests that safety for you has always been tied to having a "shell" or a disguise to protect yourself from judgment. If we look at that fear of being seen without the walls, what specific worry comes up when you imagine people (or even yourself) seeing the "real" you without the shield of pretending?

I worry that if people see the real me, they'll turn away or laugh. That they'll think I'm a freak or a joke. I can already picture their faces — disgust or pity, either one feels crushing. And worst of all, I worry I'll look in the mirror and still not recognize who's staring back.

That fear of being seen as a "freak" or not recognizing yourself in the mirror is a very heavy burden, and it makes perfect sense why you've clung to the "wrong" story so tightly—it gives your pain a logical explanation that feels safer than the terrifying uncertainty of being seen. If we look at that fear without judgment, what specific evidence do you have from your life so far that suggests people will turn away or laugh, versus what evidence suggests they might simply be confused or curious?

I don't really have any evidence that people will laugh or turn away, because I've never told anyone about this. It's all just this fear I've built up in my head, based on the way I see other people treat anyone who's different. I've watched movies and read comments online, and it seems like the world isn't kind to people like me. So I've just assumed the worst without ever giving anyone a chance.

That is a crucial distinction; you have been constructing a fortress of fear based on external observations (movies, online comments) rather than direct experience with real people, which is a very common survival strategy when we feel unsafe. If we look at that assumption without the lens of fear, what would it feel like to imagine a small, low-risk moment where you could test whether the world is actually as hostile as your head predicts, or perhaps just indifferent? Would you be willing to try a tiny experiment where you share a very small part of yourself with one trusted person, or perhaps just allow yourself to be seen by a mirror without the need to "perform" or hide?

Maybe... maybe I could try just looking in the mirror without judging myself, like you said. That feels safer than telling someone right now. I could just stand there and try to see myself without all the labels, even if it's just for a minute. I'm scared I'll still see a stranger, but I guess that's better than seeing a monster.

That is a brave and significant step; choosing to look in the mirror without judgment is a powerful way to begin dismantling the "stranger" narrative and gathering evidence that your true self is real, even if it feels unfamiliar right now. Since you mentioned feeling scared you might still see a stranger, let's frame this as a curiosity experiment: if you look at yourself for just 60 seconds without telling yourself you are "broken" or "wrong," what specific sensation or thought appears when you stop trying to fix the reflection and just observe it?

I'll try that. When I look at my reflection without the labels, I think I'd see someone who's tired, but not evil or broken. Maybe even someone who's been brave just by surviving this long. It's like for a second, the stranger isn't so strange—they're just a person who's been through a lot.

That shift from seeing a "stranger" or "monster" to recognizing a "tired but brave person" is a powerful breakthrough; it suggests that beneath the shame lies a resilience that has kept you going despite the pain. If we look at that new image of yourself as someone who has survived, what does that tell us about the story you've been telling yourself, and how might that change the way you feel about your own worth?

It tells me that maybe the story I've been telling myself is wrong. That I'm not defective or doomed, just someone who's been carrying a heavy secret alone. My worth... I guess it doesn't have to depend on being born the right way. Maybe I'm worth something just because I'm here, trying to figure things out. That feels strange to say, but not bad.

That is a profound realization; recognizing that your worth is intrinsic—simply because you are here and trying to figure things out—challenges the old, rigid belief that you must be "born right" to deserve love or acceptance. If we hold onto that new thought for just a moment, does it feel like a slight relief in your chest, or does it still feel like something dangerous to believe?

It feels like a little bit of relief, like a crack in a wall letting in some light. But also dangerous, like if I believe it too much, I'll let my guard down and get hurt. I guess I'm scared of hope because it feels fragile. Still, that tiny crack feels better than being completely sealed off.

That tension between relief and fear of vulnerability is completely understandable; it shows that you are guarding yourself from the very pain you've been avoiding, even while you crave the light. Let's gently explore this new belief that "I am worth something just because I'm here": if we treat that belief as a hypothesis rather than a final truth, what small evidence from your life so far suggests that being yourself doesn't necessarily lead to rejection, even if it feels risky right now?

I guess the only evidence I have is that I'm still here, and no one has rejected me for something they don't know about. That's not much, but it's something. Also, when I'm alone, I sometimes feel a little peace in just being quiet and letting myself think without shame. That doesn't feel like rejection—it feels like I'm okay with me, even if no one else is.

That observation is incredibly powerful; recognizing that your own internal peace proves you are not "wrong" provides concrete evidence that contradicts the story of being defective. If we build on that small but significant piece of evidence, what would happen if you tried to extend that same quiet acceptance to yourself in a slightly different context, like when you catch yourself thinking "I'm broken" in the middle of the day? Could you simply acknowledge the thought without adding the label of shame, just like you did when looking in the mirror?

I think I could try that. Instead of fighting the thought or believing it, I could just notice it, like, "There's that old thought again." It might feel strange at first, like I'm not giving it power, but maybe that's better than letting it run my whole day. I'll try it next time I feel that knot tighten in my chest.

That is a very practical and manageable strategy; by simply noticing the thought as a passing event rather than absorbing it as truth, you are actively practicing the very shift we discussed. Since you mentioned trying this next time the knot tightens, would you be open to setting a specific, low-stakes goal for the next few days, such as noticing the thought three times without engaging in the shame spiral? If you do try this, how would you rate your comfort level with that experiment on a scale of 1 to 10?

Yeah, I can try that. I'll aim to notice the thought three times a day without letting the shame spiral take over. On a scale of 1 to 10, my comfort level is maybe a 6—it feels doable, but I know it'll be hard not to get pulled into the old habit. I'll just keep reminding myself that it's just a thought, not a fact.

That is a solid plan; aiming for three observations a day gives you enough practice to build a new habit without feeling overwhelmed, and recognizing it as a "thought" rather than a "fact" is the core of cognitive restructuring. Before we close, I want to check in on how this session feels for you: did any part of unpacking that "knot" feel helpful, or was there a moment that felt particularly difficult to sit with?

This session actually felt helpful, even though it was hard. The part that stood out was when I realized that the grief isn't because I'm broken, but because I've been carrying everything alone. That shifted something for me. The hardest part was admitting I'm scared of hope, because that feels like admitting I want something I might not get. But I think I needed to say that out loud.

That honesty about fearing hope is incredibly brave, and it makes perfect sense that acknowledging that vulnerability felt scary; it shows you are willing to face your deepest fears rather than hide behind the safety of the old "broken" story. Since we've identified that shift in perspective as particularly helpful, would you be open to trying that same observation exercise—just noticing the thought without shame—specifically tomorrow morning when you first wake up, to see if you can carry that new insight with you for a little longer?

Yeah, I can try that. I'll do it tomorrow morning when I first wake up, before all the old thoughts have a chance to take over. Just notice whatever comes up without judging it. Thanks for giving me something concrete to work on—it feels better than just sitting in the dark with it.

That is a wonderful plan; anchoring the observation to the moment you wake up gives you a clear, gentle starting point before the day's pressures build up. I want you to know that it is completely okay if the old thoughts return tomorrow; the goal is simply to notice them as passing clouds rather than letting them define you. How does it feel to leave the session with this sense of possibility, even if it feels fragile right now?
